color-palette.what: A color palette is the fixed set of raw colors a product draws from, usually a gray scale plus a few hues in graded shades.
uses: Choosing colors for charts and illustrations that need several distinct categories.
Defining the colors that interface roles such as text or errors point to.
Keeping brand and data colors consistent across pages.
avoid: Coloring text, buttons or status directly from raw swatches; name colors by their job instead.
Telling chart series apart by hue alone; add labels, shapes or patterns.
practices: Keep the palette small and name every shade.
Make neighboring shades differ enough to tell apart.
Check text contrast against every background it sits on.
Give each hue the same range of light to dark steps.

semantic-colors.what: Semantic colors are named by their purpose, such as text, border, error or success, rather than by how they look. They let one design work in many themes.
uses: Coloring text, backgrounds and borders consistently across a product.
Showing status such as success, warning and error.
Switching between light and dark themes without changing components.
avoid: Picking a color for its look instead of its meaning; choose the role it plays.
Using color alone to show status; add an icon and a word.
practices: Name colors by job, not by hue.
Test each role for readable contrast in every theme.
Pair every status color with an icon and text.
Use one color per meaning, everywhere.

brand-color.what: The brand color is the one signature color that identifies a product. It marks a few key moments, such as the logo, top bar or a main button.
uses: Coloring the logo, header bar or a single main call to action.
Re-skinning a product for a new brand.
Adding a small highlight rule or accent mark.
avoid: Showing success, warning or error; use status colors instead.
Filling many elements on one screen; repeated emphasis stops standing out.
practices: Use the brand color sparingly so it keeps its impact.
Check that text on brand fills has enough contrast.
Pair it with neutral grays for most of the page.
Do not rely on it alone to show state.

accent-color.what: The accent color is the single color that signals something is interactive or selected, such as links, checked boxes and active controls.
uses: Coloring links so people see what they can click.
Showing checked, on or selected states.
Filling progress indicators and highlighting selected dates.
avoid: Coloring static headings or decorative icons; this makes people think they are clickable.
Large fills behind long text; they are hard to read.
practices: Use one action color across the whole product.
Make sure link text reaches readable contrast on every background.
Do not depend on color alone; add underlines or shapes.
Reserve the color for things people can act on.

themes.what: A theme is a complete set of colors for the same interface, such as light or dark. People choose one, or the system picks it for them.
uses: Offering a dark mode for low light or light sensitivity.
Following the person's operating system setting automatically.
Offering a low-glare paper-like reading mode.
avoid: Writing separate styles for each theme in every component; define shared color names once.
Using pure black backgrounds; very dark grays are easier on the eyes.
practices: Respect the system theme by default and remember a manual choice.
Keep contrast readable in every theme.
Define colors by role so components need no theme-specific code.
Test every screen in all themes.

typography.what: Typography is the choice and arrangement of fonts, sizes and weights so text is easy to read and its importance is clear.
uses: Setting headings, body text, labels and captions.
Showing code in a monospaced font.
Building a clear visual hierarchy on a page.
avoid: Inventing new sizes and weights for each page; use a fixed scale.
Setting long text in all capitals; use it only for short labels.
practices: Use one readable font family with few weights.
Size text in relative units so it follows the user's settings.
Limit line length to about 70 characters.
Use tabular figures for numbers in tables.

spacing.what: Spacing is the empty room around and between elements. A fixed scale of steps makes layouts consistent and shows which things belong together.
uses: Setting padding, margins and gaps between elements.
Grouping related items closer than unrelated ones.
Separating sections without lines or boxes.
avoid: Picking one-off values such as 10px or 18px; use the scale.
Using the same gap at every level; it hides the grouping.
practices: Base all spacing on one unit, such as 8px.
Work from the inside out: the smallest gap sits closest to the content.
Use space before adding borders.
Keep gaps larger between groups than within them.

borders.what: Borders are lines drawn around or between elements to outline them and separate content. A few set line weights keep them consistent.
uses: Outlining buttons, cards, alerts and fields.
Separating rows in tables and lists.
Marking the selected tab or a highlight.
avoid: Boxing every group; use spacing first and keep borders for real separation.
Using faint decorative lines as the edge of a control; controls need stronger contrast.
practices: Use only a few line weights and give each a meaning.
Give control outlines enough contrast to see.
Keep thick lines for emphasis only.
Pick line color by purpose, decorative or functional.

radii.what: Corner radii set how rounded the corners of elements are. A consistent corner style gives a product a recognizable look.
uses: Setting square or rounded corners on buttons, cards and fields.
Making circles for avatars, status dots and radio buttons.
Giving pills and progress tracks their rounded ends.
avoid: Mixing many corner styles in one screen; choose a small set.
Rounding checkboxes like radio buttons; shape tells people which is which.
practices: Define radii as named values, even for zero.
Use round shapes only for round things.
Apply the same radius to the same kind of element.
Keep nested corners visually consistent.

shadows.what: Shadows suggest depth by making an element look lifted above the page. They help show what floats, such as menus, or what can be moved.
uses: Lifting menus, dropdowns, popovers and toasts above content.
Showing a dragged item or a dialog.
Giving a card a hover lift.
avoid: Putting shadows on every card and panel; use a border or background tint.
Using heavy shadows for decoration; they add noise.
practices: Reserve shadows for things that float.
Use a few fixed levels, not custom blurs.
In dark themes, lighten the surface as well.
Keep shadows soft and subtle.

layers.what: Layers define the stacking order of elements that overlap, such as sticky headers, menus, dialogs and notifications.
uses: Keeping dropdowns above the content around them.
Making sure notifications are not hidden behind dialogs.
Placing sticky headers and sidebars correctly.
avoid: Using ever larger random z-index numbers; use named levels.
Layering many elements at once; reduce overlap where possible.
practices: Define a fixed, named stacking order in one place.
Order levels by how urgent the element is.
Reference names, not raw numbers.
Let the skip link and tooltips sit on top.

control-heights.what: Control heights are the standard sizes shared by buttons, fields and selects, so controls line up and are big enough to tap.
uses: Aligning buttons and fields in a row or toolbar.
Making denser controls for tables and filter bars.
Making larger controls for touch screens.
avoid: Mixing heights in one row of controls.
Small controls on touch screens; make targets at least 44px.
practices: Offer a few fixed heights, not custom ones.
Make touch targets at least 44px high.
Use the default height unless space is tight.
Grow controls automatically on touch devices.

motion.what: Motion is movement and transition in an interface, such as fades and slides, used to give feedback and explain what changed.
uses: Giving feedback on hover and press.
Showing something opening, arriving or closing.
Showing progress or loading.
avoid: Decorative animation that slows people down.
Long or looping effects, except loading indicators; keep feedback fast.
practices: Keep interface animations short, under about 400 milliseconds.
Use the same timing for the same kind of change.
Respect the reduced-motion setting and show the end state.
Use easing that decelerates for things that arrive.

aspect-ratio.what: An aspect ratio is the proportion of an element's width to its height. Setting it ahead of time reserves space before the content loads.
uses: Reserving room for images and video while they load.
Keeping thumbnails and cards a consistent shape.
Framing embedded maps or charts.
avoid: Leaving media without set dimensions; the page jumps when it loads.
Stretching images to fit; crop or letterbox instead.
practices: Set the ratio before the media loads.
Use common ratios such as 16:9, 4:3 and 1:1.
Crop images to fill the frame without distortion.
Write alt text for every image.

scrollbar.what: A scrollbar shows that content continues beyond the visible area and lets people move through it. Inner regions can have their own slim scrollbar.
uses: Scrolling long panels, menus and sidebars.
Scrolling code blocks and long lists inside a page.
Showing that a region holds more content.
avoid: Restyling the main page scrollbar; leave the system default.
Hiding scrollbars completely; people lose the cue that more exists.
practices: Keep scrollbars visible and with enough contrast.
Limit nested scrolling regions where possible.
Give scroll areas a clear height so the edge is obvious.
Make sure keyboard users can scroll them.

divider.what: A divider is a thin line that separates groups of content, either across a page or between side-by-side items.
uses: Separating groups in menus and panels.
Splitting groups of toolbar buttons.
Showing an 'or' between alternative options.
avoid: Putting lines between every item; use spacing or row separators.
Faking a heading with a line; use a real section title.
practices: Use dividers sparingly so they keep meaning.
Try spacing first.
Hide purely decorative lines from screen readers.
Mark real separators with the correct role.

chevron-separator.what: A chevron separator is a small arrow-like mark placed between items in a path, showing that one sits inside the other.
uses: Separating levels in breadcrumbs.
Showing file or folder paths.
Showing nested categories.
avoid: Using it as a button or toggle; use a real control.
Separating unrelated items; use spacing or a divider.
practices: Keep it small and muted.
Hide it from screen readers, since the list carries the meaning.
Flip it in right-to-left languages.
Use the same mark everywhere.

sr-only.what: Screen-reader-only text is content hidden from the screen but still read aloud by assistive technology. It supplies meaning that is otherwise only visual.
uses: Naming icon-only buttons and links.
Adding context such as 'opens in a new tab'.
Explaining changes shown only by color or arrows.
avoid: Hiding text that sighted keyboard users also need; show it.
Repeating text that is already announced.
practices: Keep hidden text short and clear.
Write it so it reads naturally in context.
Show it again when it gets keyboard focus if it is actionable.
Test with a screen reader.

skip-link.what: A skip link is a link at the very top of a page that lets keyboard and screen reader users jump past repeated navigation to the main content.
uses: Letting keyboard users bypass long menus.
Helping screen reader users reach content quickly.
Meeting basic accessibility requirements on every page.
avoid: Hiding it so it never appears when focused.
Leaving it out on pages with navigation before the content.
practices: Make it the first focusable element on the page.
Show it clearly when it gets focus.
Point it to the main content area.
Use plain wording such as 'Skip to main content'.

focus-ring.what: A focus ring is the visible outline around the element that currently has keyboard focus, showing people where they are on the page.
uses: Showing the active control during keyboard navigation.
Marking custom widgets that handle their own focus.
Helping low-vision users follow the cursor.
avoid: Removing the outline without a replacement.
Hiding it for keyboard users because it looks plain.
practices: Show it only for keyboard focus where possible.
Give it at least 3:1 contrast on every background.
Keep it thick enough to see.
Make sure it stays visible on filled controls.

chevron.what: A chevron is a small arrow that points down when a section is open and sideways when closed, hinting that the section can expand or collapse.
uses: Showing expandable accordion and disclosure sections.
Showing opened or closed tree and menu groups.
Hinting that a row reveals more.
avoid: Using it as the only sign that something is clickable; add a label.
Using it for navigation to a new page; use an arrow or link.
practices: Rotate it when the state changes.
Place it in the same spot on every row.
Expose the open state to screen readers separately.
Animate the turn briefly.

step-marker.what: A step marker is a small mark showing one step of a process, with its state such as to do, current, done or error.
uses: Showing progress through a multi-step form.
Listing stages in setup or checkout.
Showing steps on a timeline.
avoid: Using it for a single-page form; it adds noise.
Showing state by color alone; add text or an icon.
practices: Place it beside the step name.
Say the state in text for screen readers.
Mark the current step clearly.
Keep the number of steps small.

carousel-dot.what: A carousel dot is a small clickable marker for one slide in a carousel or gallery. It shows how many slides there are and which one is showing.
uses: Jumping to a specific slide.
Showing the current position in a gallery.
Letting people browse a short set of images.
avoid: Galleries with many items; show a count and thumbnails instead.
Making dots tiny to tap; keep a large target.
practices: Give each dot a label such as 'Show image 2 of 5'.
Mark the current dot by shape, not only color.
Keep dots to about eight or fewer.
Make the tap target at least 44px.

pagination-gap.what: A pagination gap is an ellipsis between page numbers showing that some pages are skipped, so long lists of pages stay short.
uses: Shortening page lists with many pages.
Keeping first, last and nearby pages visible.
Saving space in narrow layouts.
avoid: Using it when there are only a few pages; show them all.
Making it clickable; use a real page link.
practices: Show the first, last and current pages around it.
Make it non-interactive.
Hide it from screen readers.
Keep it visually quiet.

dialog-backdrop.what: A dialog backdrop is the dimmed layer behind a modal dialog. It focuses attention on the dialog and blocks the page behind it.
uses: Confirming a risky action such as delete.
Short tasks that must finish before continuing.
Asking for a decision that cannot wait.
avoid: Content people need to compare with the page; use a side panel or inline section.
Long forms; use a full page instead.
practices: Trap focus inside and return it on close.
Let Escape and a Cancel button close it.
Put actions at the bottom with the main one clear.
Dim enough to separate, but not hide the page.

drawer-backdrop.what: A drawer backdrop is the dimmed layer behind a panel that slides in from the side. Clicking it usually closes the drawer.
uses: Showing filters or settings in a side panel.
Opening navigation on phones.
Giving a large target to dismiss the drawer.
avoid: Panels people must use alongside the page; keep them docked instead.
Blocking the page without a clear way out.
practices: Let clicking the backdrop and Escape close the drawer.
Offer a visible Close button too.
Keep focus inside while it is open.
Return focus to the opener when closed.

weekday-selector.what: A weekday selector lets people pick one or more days of the week, usually with seven toggles and shortcuts for common sets.
uses: Choosing which days an event repeats.
Setting opening days or shift patterns.
Picking days for a schedule or report.
avoid: Choosing a single date; use a date picker.
Picking one day only; use a select or radio group.
practices: Offer presets such as weekdays and every day.
Start the week on the local first day.
Give each day a full accessible name.
Show clearly which days are selected.

recurrence-selector.what: A recurrence selector lets people set how an event repeats, with common choices like daily or weekly and a custom option for complex rules.
uses: Repeating calendar events and tasks.
Scheduling recurring reports or runs.
Setting repeating billing or reminders.
avoid: One-off events; do not show repeat options.
Showing every custom field up front; reveal them only when needed.
practices: Offer the most common rules first.
Name options with the real day, such as 'Weekly on Thursday'.
Summarize the custom rule in words.
Let people choose when the repeat ends.

reminder-selector.what: A reminder selector lets people choose how long before an event or deadline they are notified, and add several reminders.
uses: Setting alerts before events.
Adding notifications to tasks and deadlines.
Offering more than one reminder for one item.
avoid: Requiring a reminder; make it optional.
Free-typed times when standard offsets suffice.
practices: Offer standard time offsets.
Let people add and remove reminders.
Default to the last choice.
Cap the number of reminders.

period-selector.what: A period selector lets people choose a time range for data, such as today, this week or a custom range.
uses: Filtering reports and dashboards by time.
Switching between common time windows.
Choosing a custom date range.
avoid: Picking one exact date; use a date picker.
Long lists of periods; use a select.
practices: Show the common periods as one visible set.
Print the actual dates that result.
Make the selected period obvious.
Keep the custom option for exceptions.

granularity-selector.what: A granularity selector lets people choose how time-based data is grouped, such as by hour, day, week or month.
uses: Changing the time grouping of a chart.
Summarizing a report by week or month.
Zooming between detail and overview.
avoid: Data with no time dimension; do not offer it.
Offering groupings that would give unreadable results.
practices: Place it next to the chart it changes.
Disable choices that make no sense for the period.
Explain why a choice is unavailable.
Choose a sensible default.

calendar-view-switcher.what: A calendar view switcher lets people change how a calendar displays time, such as day, week, month or agenda.
uses: Switching between detailed and overview views of a calendar.
Viewing a list of upcoming events.
Adapting to different screen sizes.
avoid: Switching between unrelated pages; use tabs or navigation.
Offering unusual views people do not expect.
practices: Keep the selected date when switching views.
Use the standard view names.
Mark the current view clearly.
Use the agenda view by default on phones.

preset-buttons.what: Preset buttons are a row of one-tap shortcuts that fill in a more detailed control with common values.
uses: Choosing common date ranges.
Choosing common sets of days.
Filling in typical durations.
avoid: Replacing a detailed control entirely; keep it for exceptions.
Long lists of presets; use a select.
practices: Offer only a few presets.
Name them by outcome.
Show which preset matches the current value.
Keep the detailed control available.

calendar-navigation.what: Calendar navigation is a group of controls for moving to the previous or next period or jumping back to today, with a label for the period shown.
uses: Moving through weeks or months in a calendar.
Stepping through report periods.
Returning to today quickly.
avoid: Jumping far in time; add a date picker.
Leaving out the visible period label.
practices: Show the current period label.
Name arrows by period, such as 'Previous week'.
Disable Today when it is already visible.
Announce label changes politely to screen readers.

progress-bar.what: A progress bar is a horizontal track that fills to show how much of a task is done, or that animates when the time left is unknown.
uses: Showing upload, export or import progress.
Showing storage or quota use.
Showing steps completed in a task.
avoid: Waits under about a second; a spinner is enough.
Tasks with no measurable progress; use a spinner with a message.
practices: Label every bar and show the value as text.
Say what is happening for long waits.
Announce completion to screen readers.
Use color tones only with a text value.

progress-ring.what: A progress ring is a circular indicator that fills to show a percentage, often with the value in the middle.
uses: Showing completion in small tiles.
Showing a task's percent done.
Showing quota use in a compact space.
avoid: Long operations whose estimate changes; use a bar with text.
Showing precise comparisons; a bar is easier to read.
practices: Put the value in text inside or beside the ring.
Give it an accessible name.
Keep it large enough to read.
Do not rely on color alone.

spinner.what: A spinner is a small rotating icon showing that something is loading when the wait time is unknown.
uses: Showing a busy button.
Showing a field being checked.
Showing a small region loading.
avoid: Whole page loads or long waits; use a skeleton or progress bar.
Very short waits; flashing feels worse.
practices: Pair it with a short text message.
Announce it as a status to screen readers.
Keep it small and calm.
Replace it with content as soon as ready.

skeleton.what: A skeleton is a grey placeholder shaped like the content that is loading. It shows the page layout early and makes waiting feel shorter.
uses: Loading cards, lists and tables.
Loading image and video grids.
Loading sections that arrive after the page.
avoid: Content that loads almost instantly; the flash is distracting.
Waits where no layout is known; use a spinner.
practices: Match the real layout closely.
Vary line widths to look like text.
Mark the region as busy for screen readers.
Swap in content without moving the layout.
